benchmarks.name: YourMechanic (BMW 328i xDrive 2.0T)
benchmarks.note: 2013-2016 2.0L turbo estimates; page quotes shop/dealer prices of $1,762-$2,746; the same page's headline 'average $464' conflicts with its own table

finding: The live range of $270-$975 starts too low and stops a little short. Built totals (parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $353-$951 (1.0-2.5 hr); midsize 2016 Camry about $341-$1,103 (1.0-2.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $373-$987 (1.1-2.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $480-$860 (1.0-2.5 hr). The lowest total we can build is $341, and the cheapest remanufactured alternator found for any of the four vehicles was $221 before labor, so a $270 total is not realistic for a shop job; RepairPal's lowest per-model figure is $527. At the top, a list-price Toyota alternator plus 2.5 hours reaches about $1,100, in line with RepairPal's national high of $1,088, so $975 clips real quotes. A range of roughly $340-$1,100 fits mainstream vehicles better. How solid the labor times are: only the Camry has a time from its own model line (a shop quoting a 1.0 hr book time for a 2007 four-cylinder Camry). The Corolla and BMW hours come from two general statements by parts retailers (1-2 hours in most cases; 1-2.5 hours for mainstream quotes), not from a vehicle-specific source. The truck low end is a Chrysler warranty time for a 5.7L V8 car (1.1 hr) and its high end a parts seller's 2-hour install estimate. Manufacturer warranty times we found for easy-to-reach alternators are much shorter (0.5-0.6 hr on Chrysler 3.6L V6 cars and SUVs, 0.4 hr on a RAM diesel), which shows the labor on some vehicles is small, but shops bill more than warranty time. The luxury figure is the weakest and is probably too low: no BMW-specific labor time and no genuine BMW list price were found (the high part price is a remanufactured Bosch unit), and YourMechanic shows about $1,440 for a 328i 2.0T. Luxury/European and hard-to-reach alternators should be described as running well above the main range. Only Jerry's '$259-$491' headline supports the current low end, and Jerry's own table contradicts it.
extras: Quotes often add: charging-system diagnosis or battery/alternator test fee, a new serpentine belt and sometimes tensioner, a new battery if the old one was damaged by under- or over-charging, a refundable core charge on remanufactured units, battery registration/coding on some European cars, shop supplies, and sales tax.
